河西走廊历史阅读 · 连载 12 · 2026-11-04

A Coat at the Checkpoint: The Cost of a Missing Pass

关卡上的一件皮衣：缺少通行凭证的代价

一件被扣的皮衣，把汉代河西的通行规则落到了具体的人身上。

English Story

01A leather coat was taken from a traveler passing through Xuanquan, a Han relay station in the Hexi Corridor. The surviving record identifies him as Wudan, a nobleman from Weili, and says that he did not have a transport pass ready to present. It gives us neither a full hearing nor the final fate of the coat. Yet this small incident makes a large question concrete: what happened when a traveler could not show the document that officials expected? Yesterday we considered how passes and complaints reveal different parts of exchange. Today the issue is what a pass could mean for one person's possessions.

02Weili lay in the Western Regions beyond the Hexi Corridor. Xuanquan was an official station near Dunhuang, on a road used by envoys, couriers, and other travelers. These descriptions locate the episode, but they do not tell us why Wudan made this particular journey or whether he was acting for anyone else. Byung-Joon Kim discusses the incident among cases in which visitors from the west encountered Han officials over goods. The document is valuable precisely because it names a person and an object. It is also narrow: we should not turn one confiscation into a portrait of every visitor's treatment.

03A pass was more than a convenient travel note. In a system of guarded routes and official stations, written authorization helped staff decide who could proceed and what services might be supplied. Earlier installments followed an envoy's pass from Dunhuang and the records of food at Xuanquan. Wudan's case adds another possibility: an object carried by a traveler could become the subject of an official action when the expected paper was missing. That does not prove the coat was merchandise, tribute, or a gift. The source calls it a leather garment. Its role in Wudan's journey remains unknown.

04The phrase 'not ready to hand' deserves attention. Kim's account says the garment was confiscated because Wudan lacked the transport pass at that moment. It does not establish that he had never been issued one. Perhaps the document was elsewhere; perhaps he had no valid document at all. Neither possibility can be chosen from the surviving notice. This distinction matters because a missing paper at inspection and an unauthorized journey are different claims. An official might have acted on what was presented at the station, while the historian can only report what the record actually preserves.

05The broader legal setting helps explain why officials cared about papers, but it must be used carefully. Kim cites the Han Ordinance on Fords and Passes, preserved among the Zhangjiashan legal texts, for restrictions on taking particular goods such as gold, copper, and horses beyond the frontier. The ordinance shows that movement of goods could be regulated by category and direction. It does not specifically name Wudan's coat or prove which rule the station applied to it. Treating the law as background, rather than a verdict in this case, keeps the difference between a general regulation and an individual encounter visible.

06There was a human cost even when the record is brief. A coat is a usable possession, and its seizure deprived Wudan of control over it at least at that point in his journey. We need not invent weather, conversation, or his feelings to recognize the consequence. We also cannot say whether he protested, recovered the garment, or received compensation. In the camel complaint discussed yesterday, envoys could raise objections about valuation and provisions; that separate case does not tell us what happened to Wudan. The two episodes show different ways that official rules touched travelers and their property.

07The station was not merely a dot on a map between China and Central Asia. Its staff handled documents, supplies, and people whose status could affect what happened next. Jidong Yang's study of the Xuanquan manuscripts describes a road system managed closely by the early empire. Wudan's coat gives that observation a sharp edge. Administrative order could make long journeys possible, but its checks could also interrupt a person's movement or separate a person from a possession. This is a reading of the institution's effects, not evidence that every official acted alike or that every traveler faced the same risk.

08The case ends where the document ends. We know a named traveler from Weili passed Xuanquan, a leather garment was taken, and the stated reason concerned a transport pass he could not present. We do not know the final decision. That limited conclusion is enough to advance the series: the history of exchange also includes inspection, proof of permission, and the power to hold property. A next question is whether other surviving Xuanquan cases show how people challenged such actions and what outcomes were recorded. Each case will need its own documents; a shared road does not make separate lives one story.

中文译文

01一名旅人经过河西走廊的汉代驿站悬泉置时，一件皮衣被扣。留存记录称他是来自尉犁的贵族乌丹，并说他当时没有备好可供出示的通行凭证。它没有留下完整审理过程，也没有交代皮衣最终怎样处置。不过，这件小事把一个大问题落到了实处：旅人拿不出官员要求的文书，会发生什么？昨天我们讨论了凭证与申诉如何呈现交易的不同片段；今天要看的是，凭证对一个人的财物可能意味着什么。

02尉犁位于河西走廊以西的西域。悬泉置是敦煌附近的官方驿站，所在道路有使者、传递文书者及其他旅人通行。这些信息说明事件发生在哪里，却不能告诉我们乌丹此行的具体目的，或他是否代表别人办事。金秉骏在讨论西方来客因货物与汉朝官员发生交涉的案例时提到此事。这份文书的价值，恰在于留下了一个人和一件物品的名字；它的范围也很窄，不能把一次扣押写成所有来客遭遇的缩影。

03通行凭证不只是一张方便出行的便条。在设有关卡和官方驿站的道路体系中，书面许可帮助工作人员判断谁可继续前行、谁可能得到供给。本连载先前追踪了敦煌签发的使团凭证，也读过悬泉置的食物记录。乌丹一案又增加了一种可能：旅人携带的物品，在预期文书缺失时可能成为官方处置对象。这并不能证明皮衣是商品、贡物或礼物。资料只称它是一件皮衣；它在乌丹行程中的用途仍不清楚。

04“当时未备好”这一点值得留意。按照金秉骏的叙述，皮衣被扣，是因为乌丹那一刻拿不出通行凭证；资料并不能证明他从未获发凭证。文书可能放在别处，也可能根本没有有效文书。仅凭现存记载，无法在两种可能中作出选择。区别很重要：检查时拿不出文件，与整段旅程未经许可，是不同的判断。官员可能依据驿站现场出示的材料行动，历史写作者却只能陈述档案实际留下的内容。

05更广的法律背景有助于理解官员为何重视文书，但使用时必须谨慎。金秉骏援引张家山汉简保存的《津关令》：其中对黄金、铜、马等特定物品出境设有限制。这说明货物移动可能依品类和方向受到管理，却没有具体提到乌丹的皮衣，也不能证明驿站对它适用了哪一条规定。把法律放在背景位置，而不当作本案判决，才能看清一般规则与个别遭遇之间的距离。

06即使记载很短，其中仍有切实的个人代价。皮衣是可以使用的财物；被扣意味着乌丹至少在行程的那个节点失去了对它的支配。无需虚构天气、对话或他的感受，也能看见这一后果。我们同样不能断言他是否抗议、取回皮衣或得到补偿。昨天讨论的骆驼申诉中，使者能够就估价和供给提出异议；那是另一件事，不能据此推断乌丹的结局。两起事件呈现了官方规则触及旅人及其财物的不同方式。

07驿站不是中国与中亚之间地图上的一个小点。工作人员处理文书、供给和旅人；旅人的身份可能影响后续处置。杨继东对悬泉文书的研究指出，早期帝国严密管理这条道路上的往来。乌丹的皮衣让这一观察变得具体：行政秩序能够支持长途行进，检查也可能中断个人行程，或使人与财物暂时分离。这是对制度影响的分析，并非证明所有官员做法相同，或所有旅人面临同样风险。

08案件只能在文书停止的地方结束。我们知道一位有姓名、来自尉犁的旅人经过悬泉置，一件皮衣被扣，记载给出的理由与他当时无法出示通行凭证有关；最终决定则无从得知。这个有限结论已足以推进连载：交换史还包括检查、许可证明和扣留财物的权力。接下来可以追问，其他留存的悬泉案件是否记录了人们如何质疑这类处置，以及结果如何。每个案件都需要自己的文书；走在同一条路上，不会让不同人的经历自动成为一个故事。

重点表达 · Key expressions

  • transport pass — 通行凭证
  • leather garment — 皮衣
  • confiscate — 扣押
  • official station — 官方驿站
  • surviving record — 留存记录

阅读理解 · Reading check

  1. What does the record say was taken from Wudan?
  2. Does the record prove Wudan never had a pass?
  3. What happened to the coat afterward?

参考答案 · Answers

  1. A leather garment was taken when he could not present a transport pass.
  2. No. It says he did not have one ready to present at that moment.
  3. The surviving record does not establish its final fate.
